questions.question: Since voters adopted Amendment 71 in 2016, a new amendment to the Colorado Constitution faces two hurdles that initiated statutes do not. Those hurdles are:
questions.correctAnswer: Petition signatures must include at least two percent of registered voters from each of Colorado's 35 state senate districts, and the amendment needs fifty-five percent of the vote - not a simple majority - to pass
distractors: Signatures from all sixty-four counties and a two-thirds vote to pass
Approval by the governor and by the Colorado Supreme Court
A five-year waiting period and ratification by the General Assembly
questions.explanation: Amendment 71 - nicknamed 'Raise the Bar' - reacted to how easily the constitution had been amended compared with statutes. The geographic-signature rule forces statewide breadth for a campaign, and the fifty-five percent threshold applies to new constitutional amendments (measures referred by the legislature, and amendments that only repeal, are treated differently).
questions.memoryHook: Broader signatures, bigger majority: fifty-five percent and all thirty-five districts.

questions.question: The General Assembly passes a controversial new law in May. Colorado citizens who oppose it can invoke the referendum power by:
questions.correctAnswer: Filing a petition within ninety days after the legislature adjourns, signed by five percent of the votes cast for secretary of state, to suspend the law until voters decide it at an election
distractors: Asking the governor to hold a special election on the law
Suing the General Assembly in small claims court
Waiting for the next census and voting the sponsors out
questions.explanation: Article V reserves the referendum alongside the initiative - the people's veto over fresh legislation. Two categories escape it: laws the legislature deems necessary for the immediate preservation of the public peace, health, or safety, and appropriation bills for the ordinary support of government. Everything else can be sent to the voters.
questions.memoryHook: Ninety days, five percent, law on hold - the referendum is the people's veto.

questions.question: A ballot question reaches Colorado voters after the General Assembly itself voted to send a proposed constitutional change to the people, with no citizen petition involved. A classmate calls it an initiative. The precise correction is:
questions.correctAnswer: It is a referred measure, not an initiative - the legislature referred it; initiatives originate with citizen petitions
distractors: It is an initiative because all ballot questions are initiatives
It is a referendum because the legislature acted within ninety days
It is a recall of the General Assembly as a body
questions.explanation: Colorado ballots carry three distinct species of question: initiatives (citizen-drafted and citizen-petitioned), referred measures (placed on the ballot by the General Assembly, which must refer all constitutional amendments it proposes), and referendums (citizen petitions against a new law). Knowing who sent the question - voters or legislature - identifies which one it is.
questions.memoryHook: Ask who sent it to the ballot: citizens petitioning means initiative, legislature sending means referral.

questions.question: The recall power in Colorado allows voters to:
questions.correctAnswer: Remove an elected official from office before the term ends, by petition followed by a special election
distractors: Force the governor to veto a bill the voters dislike
Appeal a court ruling to a statewide jury
Shorten the terms of all officials in an election year
questions.explanation: Article XXI of the Colorado Constitution extends direct democracy from laws to officeholders: if enough voters sign, the official must face the electorate mid-term. The ballot asks first whether to recall, then who should succeed if the recall succeeds.
questions.memoryHook: Recall is the mid-term election voters can schedule themselves.

questions.question: To force a recall election against a Colorado state official, petitions must carry signatures equal to at least what share of the votes cast for that office at the last election - and 2013 showed the power is real when:
questions.correctAnswer: Twenty-five percent; that year voters recalled two state senators, including the Senate president, over new gun laws - the first successful legislative recalls in state history
distractors: Five percent; that year voters recalled the governor for the first time
Fifty percent; that year the entire General Assembly faced recall
Ten percent; that year voters recalled a Colorado Supreme Court justice
questions.explanation: The twenty-five percent threshold is deliberately steep - recalls are for genuine revolts, not rematches. In September 2013, Senate President John Morse of Colorado Springs and Senator Angela Giron of Pueblo were both removed after supporting post-Aurora and Sandy Hook gun legislation, proving Article XXI is a working tool, not a museum piece.
questions.memoryHook: One voter in four from the last election signs - and in 2013, two senators went home early.

questions.question: Colorado's Taxpayer's Bill of Rights - TABOR, added to the state constitution by voters in 1992 - is famous for requiring governments in Colorado to get what before raising taxes?
questions.correctAnswer: Approval from the voters themselves at an election
distractors: Permission from the governor's budget office
A ruling from the Colorado Supreme Court
Consent of the U.S. Treasury Department
questions.explanation: TABOR (Article X, Section 20) is the most consequential amendment in modern Colorado government: new taxes, tax-rate increases, and most debt require a public vote. Supporters prize the direct control; critics note it is why Colorado's constitution, not its legislature, hosts so much fiscal policy.
questions.memoryHook: In Colorado, tax hikes go to the ballot first - TABOR wrote the voters into the budget.

questions.question: In a strong economy, Colorado state revenue grows faster than TABOR's limit - generally the prior year's revenue adjusted for inflation plus population growth. Under TABOR, the state must generally:
questions.correctAnswer: Refund the excess revenue to taxpayers (or obtain voter approval to keep and spend it), rather than simply retaining the surplus
distractors: Deposit all excess revenue in a permanent trust the voters may never touch
Transfer the excess to the federal government
Use the excess only to retire the governor's office expenses
questions.explanation: The refund mechanism is TABOR's engine: growth beyond inflation-plus-population does not belong to the state unless voters say so - in the 2005 Referendum C, voters did approve a five-year timeout from the cap. Surpluses within the limit are ordinary revenue; the rule bites only at the ceiling.
questions.memoryHook: Grow past inflation plus population and the extra goes back - unless voters vote to keep it.

questions.question: Colorado's path to legal marijuana was built entirely through the initiative process. Which pairing is correct?
questions.correctAnswer: Amendment 20 (2000) legalized medical marijuana; Amendment 64 (2012) legalized recreational use and possession for adults twenty-one and older
distractors: Amendment 64 (2000) legalized medical use; Amendment 20 (2012) legalized recreational use
Both changes were ordinary statutes passed by the General Assembly in 2014
Marijuana was legalized by a Colorado Supreme Court ruling in 2012
questions.explanation: Both measures amended Article XVIII of the state constitution by citizen initiative - medical first, then, in 2012, personal use for adults, making Colorado (with Washington, the same night) the first state to legalize recreational marijuana. The sequence is the standard classroom exhibit of initiatives building policy step by step.
questions.memoryHook: 2000 medical, 2012 recreational - two initiatives, twelve years apart.

questions.question: Colorado's government-to-government relationship in state civics centers on the state's two federally recognized tribal nations headquartered within its borders. They are:
questions.correctAnswer: The Southern Ute Indian Tribe and the Ute Mountain Ute Tribe
distractors: The Northern Arapaho Tribe and the Eastern Shoshone Tribe
The Navajo Nation and the Jicarilla Apache Nation
The Cheyenne and Arapaho Tribes of Oklahoma
questions.explanation: The Southern Ute Indian Tribe (headquartered at Ignacio) and the Ute Mountain Ute Tribe (headquartered at Towaoc) hold reservations in southwestern Colorado. The 2022 Colorado Academic Standards and section 22-1-104's civics course expect students to study exactly this relationship; tribes like the Navajo Nation border Colorado but are headquartered in other states.
questions.memoryHook: Two tribal nations headquartered in Colorado: Southern Ute and Ute Mountain Ute.

questions.question: A Colorado state trooper wants to enforce a state regulation against a tribal citizen for conduct entirely on the Southern Ute Reservation. The tribal government objects that the state lacks authority there. The objection rests on the principle that:
questions.correctAnswer: Tribes are sovereign governments whose authority over their territory and citizens predates the United States; state power on reservations is limited, and the relationship runs government-to-government
distractors: Reservations are counties of the state and must follow all state directives
Tribal governments are private associations with no governmental status
The state may act freely because the reservation lies within state borders
questions.explanation: Tribal sovereignty is inherent - retained, not granted by Washington - and the U.S. Supreme Court has treated tribes as distinct political communities since the 1830s. Colorado works with the Southern Ute and Ute Mountain Ute through the Colorado Commission of Indian Affairs and formal agreements, precisely because ordinary state jurisdiction does not simply extend onto the reservation.
questions.memoryHook: Sovereignty came first: the state's power stops where tribal self-government governs.

questions.question: Both Colorado Ute tribes operate casinos on their reservations. The legal arrangement that makes this possible is best described as:
questions.correctAnswer: Tribal-state gaming compacts negotiated under the federal Indian Gaming Regulatory Act - agreements between sovereigns, not state licenses granted to businesses
distractors: Ordinary state casino licenses issued by the Colorado Division of Gaming
A TABOR amendment authorizing tribal casinos by popular vote
County zoning variances for reservation entertainment venues
questions.explanation: The Indian Gaming Regulatory Act (1988), passed after the Supreme Court's Cabazon decision affirmed tribal gaming rights, requires tribes and states to negotiate compacts for casino-style gaming in good faith. Colorado's compacts with the Southern Ute and Ute Mountain Ute tribes are government-to-government agreements - the compact form itself is a lesson in tribal sovereignty.
questions.memoryHook: A compact between sovereigns, not a license from the state - that is how tribal gaming is built.
